::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How is $-u''(t)/u'(t) > 0$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2502282/how-is-ut-ut-0), asked by [K. Sepoko](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/498711/k-sepoko) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-11-03; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I am faced with the following problem $-u''(t)/u'(t) > 0$. This equation is in a mathematical article related to soil degeneration. Can someone please explain how this is possible.
:::

The negative sign on the left-hand side doesn't mean the left-hand side is negative.  Basically we need $u'(t)$ and $u''(t)$ to have opposite signs.  Then their quotient is negative, and the opposite of it is positive.

So a function $u$ with $u'>0$ and $u''<0$ (i.e., increasing and concave down) will satisfy the inequality.  Or a function with $u'<0$ and $u''>0$ (i.e., decreasing and concave up).

Explicitly, both $u(t) = \sqrt{t}$ and $u(t) =\frac{1}{t}$ would work.
